subtype: Being told it was own fault [Receiver]
passage: Parul, sit, let me tell you something since you're starting college. When I was a young man of twenty, I got a letter saying I'd won a scooter in a lucky draw. Just pay a small "delivery fee" by money order, it said. I sent almost my whole month's hostel money. No scooter came, of course. When I told my elder brother, he laughed and said, "Harish, you're a fool. Who wins scooters? You deserved to lose it." I didn't eat properly for days, not from hunger but from shame. It was my roommate Jacob who sat with me, said, "They're thieves, you're not stupid," and walked with me to the post office and the police chowki to report it. The money never came back. But the shame slowly left.

qa.q: What did Harish's elder brother say when he heard about the lost money?
qa.a: He laughed and said, "Harish, you're a fool. Who wins scooters? You deserved to lose it."

qa.q: Why did Harish not eat properly for days?
qa.a: His brother's words made him feel ashamed, as if being cheated proved he was stupid, so the loss turned into a heavy sense of his own fault.

qa.q: Which choice of Jacob's turned things around for Harish?
qa.a: Jacob named the cheats as the thieves and then walked with Harish to the post office and the police chowki, so listening came with real steps.

qa.q: How might things have gone if the elder brother had reacted the way Jacob did?
qa.a: Harish would likely have felt less alone and ashamed, and might not have spent days hardly eating.

grounding: An elder recalls being told a scam was his own fault, and how a friend's listening and practical help eased the shame.

subtype: Being told it was own fault [Receiver]
passage: Sabina's phone showed eight percent battery when she realised the "internship registration fee" had vanished along with the recruiter's number. The power was out in the whole hostel lane because of the storm. She called her cousin first. "Sabina, seriously? Anyone smart would have checked. You basically handed it over," he said, and hung up to take another call. She sat on the stairs with her face hot, thinking maybe he was right, maybe she was just gullible. Bhupen, from the next room, came down with a torch and a power bank. He listened to the whole thing without interrupting. Then he said, "Plug in. First, the bank's card-block number. Then we file it on the cybercrime portal before the battery dies." They finished the complaint at 11:40 by torchlight.

qa.q: What did Bhupen bring down to the stairs?
qa.a: Bhupen came down with a torch and a power bank.

qa.q: What was Sabina thinking after her cousin's call, and why?
qa.a: She wondered if she was just gullible, because his "anyone smart would have checked" made the loss feel like her failing, not the scammer's.

qa.q: Which choice of Bhupen's made the difference that night?
qa.a: He listened without interrupting before giving steps, then helped her block the card and file the complaint despite the storm and low battery.

qa.q: What would change if Bhupen had echoed the cousin instead of listening?
qa.a: Sabina might have stayed frozen in shame on the dark stairs, and with the battery dying the complaint might never have been filed.

grounding: A young woman cheated by a fake internship is blamed by her cousin, then helped by a neighbour's listening and practical steps.

subtype: Being told it was own fault [Receiver]
passage: In the Andheri flat, Madhav finally told the family at dinner: he had paid a "seller" on a chat app for a used laptop, and the seller had blocked him. Papa put down his roti. "Twenty-one years old and you fall for this? You should've been smarter. That's your whole problem." Madhav stared at his dal and said nothing for the rest of the meal. Later his cousin Shankar knocked and sat on the edge of the bed. "Tell me how it happened, from the start." Madhav told him, voice cracking at the part where he'd sent the money. Shankar nodded. "They do this for a living. Screenshot the chat, and tomorrow morning we'll go to the cyber cell together." Madhav opened the chat and started saving screenshots.

qa.q: What did Madhav pay the "seller" for?
qa.a: He paid a "seller" on a chat app for a used laptop, and the seller blocked him.

qa.q: What does Madhav's silence over his dal suggest he felt after Papa spoke?
qa.a: It suggests shame: "You should've been smarter" made him feel the loss was proof of his own foolishness.

qa.q: What turning point got Madhav moving again?
qa.a: When Shankar asked him to tell it from the start and then named a plan, screenshots and a visit to the cyber cell, Madhav began saving the chat.

qa.q: How might Papa's reaction come from his own worry, and what does it cost?
qa.a: Papa may be scared and angry about the money, but blaming Madhav at dinner made his son go silent instead of asking for help.

grounding: A young man scammed over a laptop is blamed by his father and then steadied by a cousin who listens and plans next steps.

subtype: Being told it was own fault [Receiver]
passage:
'Nine thousand? For a "registration fee"?' Ramesh put down his tea. 'Jatin, you're doing a degree. How could you fall for that?'
Jatin stared at the floor. 'The letter had a logo. The man on the phone knew my college's name.'
'Anyone could find that. You should have been smarter.'
'I know!' Jatin's voice cracked. 'You think I haven't said that to myself fifty times since morning?'
Maa came in from the kitchen, wiping her hands. 'Ramesh. Enough.'
Silence. Ramesh rubbed his face. 'Sorry, chhote. That was my fright talking. Show me the messages.'
Jatin held out the phone.
'Okay. We call the bank helpline now, then report it to the cyber police tonight. Screenshot everything.' Ramesh paused. 'These people do this for a living. It's on them.'
Jatin let out a long breath.

qa.q: How much did Jatin pay as a 'registration fee'?
qa.a: Nine thousand.

qa.q: How does Jatin feel when Ramesh says 'You should have been smarter', and what shows it?
qa.a: Jatin feels deep shame: Jatin's voice cracks, and Jatin admits to having said the same thing fifty times since morning.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the conversation, and what practical steps followed?
qa.a: Maa's 'Enough' and Ramesh's apology; Ramesh then asked to see the messages and planned to call the bank helpline, report it to the cyber police and screenshot everything.

qa.q: Why might Ramesh have snapped at first, and what changed his stance?
qa.a: Ramesh calls it 'my fright talking': the fear about the loss came out as blame; once Maa stopped him, he put the responsibility on the scammers, not Jatin.

grounding: A young person cheated by a fake job fee is told they should have been smarter, and then gets listening and practical steps at home.

subtype: Being told it was own fault [Receiver]
passage:
Last October I paid a stranger four thousand rupees for a room near campus that didn't exist. The photos were real, just stolen. When I told my hostel floor, one girl laughed: 'Who pays without seeing it? Be smarter, Ira.' Someone else said I'd basically gifted it. I stopped eating in the mess for a few days because I felt everyone knew.
Pema was different. She sat on my bed and let me tell the whole stupid story without a single 'but why did you'. Then she opened her laptop. 'Okay. Bank first, then the cyber complaint, then we warn the housing group so nobody else gets caught.'
I only got half the money back. But what I remember most isn't the loss. It's that someone treated me as the person who was tricked, not the person who was dumb.

qa.q: How much did Ira pay for the room that didn't exist?
qa.a: Four thousand rupees.

qa.q: Why did Ira stop eating in the mess for a few days?
qa.a: Ira felt ashamed after being laughed at and told to be smarter, and believed everyone knew; the blame piled shame on top of the loss.

qa.q: Which of Pema's choices helped Ira most, and why?
qa.a: Listening to the whole story without 'but why did you', then working through the bank, the cyber complaint and a warning to the housing group; support came first, then practical steps.

qa.q: How might the girl who said 'Be smarter, Ira' see it differently if she had been tricked the same way?
qa.a: She would likely feel how much 'be smarter' stings on top of losing money, and see that the stranger who faked the listing did the wrong, not the person fooled.

grounding: A student cheated over a fake room is blamed as foolish by some, while a friend's listening and practical help lets them recover.
